prompts.q: Name a way to achieve cost leadership
prompts.hint: Standardise, scale up, get efficient, innovate, cheap inputs
prompts.learn: Cost leadership means striving to be the lowest-cost producer and the most price-competitive business in the market. It is one of the two strategic roles of operations; the other is good/service differentiation.

answers.why: Producing on a larger scale cuts the cost per unit, e.g. through bulk-buying inputs.
More output from the same inputs (lean production, less wastage) lowers unit costs.
Uniform, mass-produced goods are cheaper to make than customised ones.
Buying inputs overseas where they cost less reduces input costs.
Innovative, cost-efficient production methods cut processing costs.
Machines and robots replace labour, removing a major cost in the long term.
Sole access to cheap raw materials gives a cost edge rivals can't copy.
Placing larger orders with fewer suppliers wins economies of scale (a Finance link).

near.msg: That's the other strategic role, differentiation, which usually raises costs.
Higher quality usually adds cost; cost leaders often sacrifice some quality instead.
That's the goal of cost leadership; name a way to get there, e.g. economies of scale.

prompts.q: Name a way to differentiate a good or service
prompts.hint: Goods: features, quality, design, extras. Services: time, expertise
prompts.learn: Differentiation means modifying products so they are unique and distinct from competitors' products. It is the alternative strategic role to cost leadership and usually increases costs.

answers.why: Adding functions competitors lack makes the product stand out.
Superior materials and workmanship set the product apart.
Distinctive styling or built-in technology competitors can't match.
Tailoring the good or service to each customer's needs.
Extras beyond the core product, such as a warranty or after-sales service.
Services can stand out by how quickly they are delivered.
Services differ by the skill, qualifications and experience of the provider.
Partnerships add benefits, e.g. Woolworths-Caltex fuel deals or Qantas-Emirates code-sharing.

near.msg: Competing on low price is cost leadership, the other strategic role.

answers.why: A service can't be touched, e.g. a haircut or financial advice.

prompts.q: Name a feature of FIFO
prompts.hint: Oldest first: think rotation AND valuation
prompts.learn: First-in-first-out (FIFO) moves the oldest stock to the front so it is used or sold first. As a valuation method in times of inflation, it gives lower COGS, higher gross profit and closing stock at recent prices.

answers.why: Stock that arrives first is moved to the front and used first.
Stock is used before it expires, reducing waste.
Best for goods with expiry dates or that date quickly (tech, fashion).
Newer deliveries go behind or beneath existing stock.
Shelf stackers put new stock at the back to prevent spoilage.
Older, cheaper stock is expensed first.
Lower COGS means higher gross profit when prices rise.
Gives a stronger balance sheet position.

near.msg: That describes LIFO, not FIFO.

prompts.q: Name a feature of LIFO
prompts.hint: Newest first, and banned for valuation in Australia
prompts.learn: Last-in-first-out (LIFO) uses or sells the newest stock first, often unavoidably with bulk goods like fuel or gravel. As a valuation method it is prohibited in Australia under AASB 102.

answers.why: Newer deliveries go on top or in front and are drawn first.
Fine where age doesn't affect quality.
Older stock can stay at the back indefinitely and spoil.
New fuel sits above old; gravel is added to and taken from the top.
Newer, dearer stock is expensed first.
A consequence of storage methods, not a deliberate choice.
Higher COGS means lower gross profit when prices rise.
Gives a weaker balance sheet position.
LIFO valuation is banned under accounting standard AASB 102 Inventories.

near.msg: That describes FIFO, not LIFO.

prompts.q: Name a quality control technique
prompts.learn: Quality control uses inspections at points in the production process to check for defects against predetermined standards. It is reactive, unlike proactive quality assurance (e.g. ISO 9000) and quality improvement.

answers.why: Checking products at various points in production.
Tests designed to assess products against predetermined standards.
Checking a sample of output rather than every unit.
X-rays detect hidden defects, cutting warranty claims.
Photos and other imaging spot defects.
For services, inspecting how employees deliver the service.
Infrared detects defects the eye can't see.

near.msg: ISO accreditation is quality assurance: a proactive system, not inspection.
That's quality improvement, a proactive approach.

prompts.q: Name a quality improvement strategy
prompts.hint: Kaizen, TQM, Six Sigma and more
prompts.learn: Quality improvement is a proactive commitment to continuous improvement and total quality management. Six Sigma's five steps are define, measure, analyse, improve and control.

answers.why: An ongoing commitment to improve products and processes.
Every employee is responsible for quality: benchmarking, empowerment, customer focus.
Training lifts staff skills (a link with HR).
Removes the causes of errors: define, measure, analyse, improve, control.
Gathers customer insights on quality.
Workers doing similar jobs meet regularly to solve work problems.
Staff from different functions work together on a problem.
Aiming for no defects at all.
Evaluating the efficiency of an operational process.
A problem-solving technique using employee ideas.

near.msg: That's quality control: reactive inspection, not improvement.
ISO accreditation is quality assurance.

prompts.q: Name a cause of resistance to change in operations
prompts.learn: Resistance to change comes from financial costs (purchasing new equipment, redundancy payments, retraining, reorganising plant layout) and the psychological pull of inertia: PIF RRR.

answers.why: Change costs money: equipment, payouts, training, downtime.
High cost, though it can be leased (dearer long term).
Costly and time-consuming when roles or technology change.
Required by law; higher with long service, high pay and unused leave.
Downtime and the cost of physical reorganisation can be substantial.
A natural tendency to resist change from fear of the unknown, even in management.

near.msg: That's a strategy for overcoming resistance, not a cause of it.

prompts.q: Name a way to overcome resistance to change
prompts.learn: Change management means identifying the source of change, communicating why it is needed, building a culture of change and using change agents. Leasing equipment can soften the upfront financial cost.

answers.why: Staff who understand why are more supportive.
Training staff in new technology or roles eases the change.
If staff are included, they are more likely to support change.
A person or group who drives and manages the change process.
A culture that expects and welcomes change.
Avoids the high upfront cost of buying, though dearer long term.
Find the (usually external) source and assess whether change is needed.

near.msg: That's a cause of resistance, not a way to overcome it.

prompts.q: Name a way operations can scan and learn
prompts.learn: Scanning and learning means studying the world's best operational processes in your industry and applying them. It is one of four global factors (REGS): research and development, economies of scale, global sourcing, scanning and learning.

answers.why: Scanning other businesses worldwide for best practice.
Industry conferences share new methods.
Employees who have worked in other businesses or countries bring ideas.
Taking rivals' products apart to learn how they are made.
Journals publish the latest operations research.
Forums let operations managers swap knowledge.

near.msg: That's one of the other global factors (REGS), not scanning and learning.
